>
> OK, so what happens with before range with this example:
>
> Meth 1: I rush X at Y stealth
> Meth 2: Action Sucessful
> Meth 1: Before range I play weather control
> Meth 2: I play torn signpost
> Meth 1: I play increased strength
> Meth 2: I play increased strength
> Meth 1: I play flesh of marble
> Meth 2: I play nothing
> Meth 1: I play nothing
>
> What happens here?

As Chris mentioned, priority for playing cards during any particular game
phase or step is generally: acting Methuselah first, then blocking (or
other) Methuselah(s) afterwards. The rulebook section 1.6.1.5 "Sequencing"
(in the "Overview of Library Cards, General" section) describes the rules
for this.

In fact, the sequencing rules don't usually result in the card-plays you
describe above taking place in the sequence you've ordered them there. This
is because *every time* more than one player wants to do something, the
acting Meth has priority. After playing her first effect, she gets priority
again to play the next effect, and continues playing effects until she's
done and declares "pass". Then the blocking (or other) Meth gets priority
and can play an effect - however, the acting Meth gets priority back as soon
as "Meth 2" does play an effect, and can play more effects if she wishes.
In practice it is common for the acting Meth to not explicitly declare that
she's passing on opportunities to play additional cards every time the
blocking Meth wants to play a card, but she does have the ability to
"interrupt" after each play if she wishes.

Note that this doesn't mean that the acting Meth's effects are
un-interruptable: if there are effects that are necessarily played in
reaction to her effects (e.g. Direct Intervention against the Weather
Control), the blocking Meth does have the opportunity to "interrupt". But
the blocking Meth doesn't get to play any "general" (i.e. non-special-case)
effects until the acting Meth is done playing all of her general effects.

So the sequence you describe should usually, instead, go like this:

Meth 1: I rush X at Y stealth
Meth 2: Action Sucessful
Meth 1: Before range I play weather control

Meth 1: I also play increased strength
Meth 1: I also play flesh of marble
Meth 1: I play nothing else at this time
[then]

Meth 2: I play torn signpost

[Meth 1: I play nothing]

Meth 2: I play increased strength

[Meth 1: I play nothing]

Meth 2: I play nothing

When both Methuselahs have passed in succession, the phase (or step or
whatever) ends and you move to the next step.

Of course, it *could* happen a different way, if the acting Meth isn't
interested in playing Flesh of Marble until Meth 2 has surprised Meth 1 by
whipping out the Torn Signpost, for example. In that case it might go like:

Meth 1: I rush X at Y stealth
Meth 2: Action Sucessful
Meth 1: Before range I play weather control

Meth 1: I also play increased strength
Meth 1: I play nothing else at this time
[then]

Meth 2: I play torn signpost

[Meth 1: I play flesh of marble]
[Meth 1: I play nothing else at this time]

Meth 2: I play increased strength

[Meth 1: I play nothing]

Meth 2: I play nothing

This is also why, if the acting Meth is interested in using an action
modifier to increase bleed, but the target Meth is considering playing
Deflection, there is no stalemate: if the acting Meth plays Conditioning,
the target Meth can then play Deflection (when the acting Meth is done
declaring effects), but if the acting Meth passes (wanting to see if the
target Meth plays Deflection), and the target Meth *declines* to play
Deflection, the phase for playing those effects has ended (because both
Meths have passed) and the acting Meth cannot *then* play Conditioning. Or
to

> Alternativly:
>
> Meth 1: I play protected resources
> Meth 2 I bleed Meth 1 for 2
> Meth 1: I decline to block
> Meth 2: I jack the bleed to 5
> Meth 1 I play telepathic counter
>
> What happens here?

In this case, it might look more like:

Meth 1: [has Protected Resources in play]

Meth 2: I bleed Meth 1 for 2
Meth 1: I decline to block
Meth 2: I jack the bleed to 5

Meth 1: I play telepathic counter at superior
Meth 2: I don't increase the bleed any further
Meth 1: I burn 2 pool for the bleed that resolves at 3 (due to P.R.)

Does this answer your questions at all? You're right to suspect that there
are some subtleties to the timing of effects in VTES, but almost all of them
are resolved by who the rulebook says has priority at any given moment, and
what the particular card-texts are (e.g. Protected Resources' effect is
that, no matter how large the bleed is that's coming at you, you will only
burn 2 pool when the bleed resolves).

Josh

ordering the "before range" effect in. He can only pass when he has
nothing else to do.

play any number of other effects - but would have to order in the
Weather Control before passing.

Thank you gentlemen.
So what this boils down to is that the acting Meth maintains priority,
with the ability to order any effects that he/she plays. After playing
X cards, target Meth gets priority and can play X effects, ordering
them as he/she wants. After this, acting Meth regains priority and
sequence repeats until both Meths decline to play any more effects.
Additionaly, if any said effects have mandatory effects, these must be
ordered by the acting Meth no matter who plays them. Finally any effect
that can cancel another effect must be played after the "offending"
effect is played as this is the window for doing so.

Messages.Author: ira...@gmail.com
Messages.Body:


Looks good, except that the "target Meth gets priority and can play X
effects," should really be "target Meth gets priority and can play one
effect, after which the acting Meth regains priority (and can then pass
back to the target Meth.)"

The playthrough that Josh gave for combat and bleeds in your example
were good. The Target Meth can always ask the question to the Acting
Meth, "Do you have anything else to play at this time?" The Acting
Meth, after playing all the cards he wants to play, will eventually
say, "No." Then, the Target Meth can either play a card (and priority
goes back to the Acting Meth), or not (and then the window closes and
you move on to the next step.)

You're right. Psyche! is an unusual case because, by its own card-text, the
superior effect is not played during combat even though it is a combat card.
That is, the first combat has to have already ended for you to be able to
start a new one (you can't start a new combat while the old combat is still
going on). That's why Marthe can't retrieve a superior Psyche! with her
ability: the Psyche! wasn't played "during" either of the two combats, if
she plays it at superior. (She *can* retrieve a Psyche! if she uses it to
press (the [cel] effect) in combat 1, after combat 1 ends, and then
immediately play that same Psyche! at superior to start combat 2. But after
combat 2 ends, she would not be able to again put it in your hand, because
the second time, it wasn't played during combat.)

This timing is, as you say, kinda weird. The fact that it has a basis in
card-text makes it make sense to me, at least. :-)

Josh

As others have noted, this is legal.

A common response to the stealing action is to "spike" the card by tapping
it to put a useless card from your prey's ash heap on it. The best cards for
this purpose are "once per game" effects that have already been played, like
Giant's Blood or Ancient Influence, but a discipline that the stealing
Meth's vamps can't play is almost as good.

- Pat
